activity.title: SO AMAZING!

Today we're launching Hatch Sleep Clock. For over a decade, Hatch has helped people fall asleep. Every night, more than 2 million people use one to wind down and to wake up. Now, for the first time, it can tell us how people actually slept once the lights went off. That means we can finally help with the part in between falling asleep and waking up, not just the two bookends. Hatch Sleep Clock is a sleep tracker built right into the device, fully contactless, nothing to wear and nothing to charge. It's still the same routine people already love: the sound, the light, the story that gets you to sleep. Except now, it also tracks how you actually slept, so we can help you sleep better, night after night. This is the next chapter of something we've been building since 2014. Sleep has always been our constant. This is just the next way we get to help with it. https://lnkd.in/gde-8pwp

When I declared symbolic systems as my major six years ago, I honestly didn't really know what it meant. I liked the idea of taking classes across CS, philosophy, psych, linguistics, HCI. A clear case of decision paralysis… Sue me! By the end of my time at Stanford, it became clear to me why I gravitated toward the major. Symsys has always been about one question: how do humans and machines learn and reason? That question has shaped almost everything I've worked on. I explored it through Margins , documenting culture through fashion. Then within climate and energy, researching the infrastructure powering the AI boom. Now it's brought me to Simile ! Simile is a frontier AI lab building foundation models of human behavior. We build AI simulations grounded in real people so organizations can explore one of the hardest questions in decision making: what happens if...? What happens if we launch this product? Enter this market? Write this policy? And just as importantly, what happens if we don't? Instead of relying on limited research or intuition, organizations can rehearse consequential decisions before making them in the real world. Today, that means helping businesses make better decisions, faster. Tomorrow, the same technology could help us better understand everything from epidemic response and disaster planning to the downstream effects of economic policy. As much as this is a technical AI challenge, it's equally a design challenge. How should people interact with simulations? How do you make this new experience intuitive and delightful? And how do you know when to trust the results? Simulation sits at the intersection of machine reasoning and the messiness of human behavior, which is exactly what made me fall in love with symsys in the first place! I'm excited to be joining the GTM team, helping scale simulation across enterprises while also working on our comms and branding. It's hard to imagine a better team to invent the wheel with. Joon Sung Park , Lainie Yallen , Michael Bernstein , and Percy Liang have helped pioneer the field of generative agents, AI simulation, and foundation models. After just a few weeks here, it's clear how creative, thoughtful, and ambitious this team is. If you're as excited about the possibilities of simulation as I am, please reach out!!

I just graduated from Stanford, and surprisingly, I feel happier, more energized, and more excited than ever. The SF bubble can be an echo chamber. In search of more original, creative, and grounded thinking, I’m moving to New York to join AMI - Advanced Machine Intelligence alongside Yann LeCun , Saining Xie , and an incredible team researching on world modeling and physical intelligence. Excited to branch out and meet people from all walks of life in NYC. Please reach out :)

Today, my sister Farah U. and I closed a $30M Series A! We’re announcing Nectar Social ’s $30M Series A led by Amy Wu Martin at Menlo Ventures and its Anthology Fund (in partnership with Anthropic), with True Ventures , GV (Google Ventures) , and Gwyneth Paltrow 's Kinship Ventures, LLC . Thank you to Lucinda Shen at Axios for breaking the story. When Farah and I started Nectar, we kept coming back to the same observation. The conversations that actually shape what people buy have moved into DMs, comments, group chats, and creator posts. Places no human team can realistically staff. AI has created infinite content. Brands now need infinite presence. But the marketing software stack wasn't built for this world. It was built for an era when the work happened on an interface, in business hours, by a team big enough to keep up. None of those things are true anymore. Engineering has already lived through this shift. Developers stopped writing every line of code and started directing agents that execute against outcomes. Marketing is in the same moment now. The teams that win the next decade won't be the ones who staff harder. They'll be the ones who direct intelligent systems that show up everywhere customers already are, in the brand's voice, in real time, with the team's judgment built in. That's what Nectar Agent does. As Ekta Chopra , Chief AI Officer at e.l.f. Cosmetics recently shared, "The software stack most brands built was designed for an era when the work happened on the interface. That's no longer true. At e.l.f. Beauty, social is where discovery, decision, and loyalty actually happen. Nectar has combined our customer experience, influencer, social marketing, and insights work into one operating system, lifted response rates 60%, and given us the first clean line from a social conversation to revenue. Connected commerce isn't a vision anymore. This is what it looks like in production." Nectar already powers more than 10 million conversations a week for brands like e.l.f., Babylist, Liquid Death, Graza, Caraway, Kosås, Goop, Crown Affair, and Tower 28. We've attributed $100M+ in revenue back to social, engaged 50M+ consumers, and grown 5x in the last three months alone. Thank you to every customer, partner, investor, and Nectar teammate who got us here. We're just getting started. Axios link in the comments 👇

Inspired by Garry Tan 's gstack, I built AskLeo, a free tool that evaluates your startup idea the way a VC would. A lot of first-time founders and students have reached out over the years asking for feedback on their ideas. I can't always respond to everyone, so I built this instead. Over the past few years I've watched remarkable deep-tech founders come out of Y Combinator and grow faster than anyone expected. Philip Johnston and the Starcloud team are a perfect example, building data centers in space and becoming the fastest unicorn in YC history just 17 months after demo day. That kind of execution is exactly why we keep coming back to Y Combinator . YC just dropped their Summer 2026 Requests for Startups. If you're thinking about applying or just stress-testing an idea, I built something that might help. I've reviewed thousands of companies as a GP at FoundersX Ventures . I distilled that into a framework covering the questions most first-time founders haven't thought through: market sizing, competition, team fit, IP, regulatory path, data moat, path to $100M ARR. One question at a time, constructively. Try it here → https://lnkd.in/eEhi_4WF (It is a Claude artifact, runs in your own Claude, so I don't have access to your data). Still improving. The hidden talent of a Senior Director of Product Management at Meta is... Cake. Fun fact: Sean Liu builds hardware at Meta by day, and has a passion for elaborate cakes. Has even appeared on The Great American Baking Show. Last night in Palo Alto a small group sat down for dinner with folks from JZ's Product Management course at Stanford. Big tech used to come with the promise of status, scale, and certainty. An early stage startup offers power, influence, and autonomy. People (used to) pick one or the other based on where they are in their career and what they want from the next few years, and we discussed what each one of us is currently focused on. What's now changing is the shape and size of organizations and individual teams. Sean described how Meta is reorganizing around agentic orchestration. Pods of five or six people are building, each running many agents in parallel. His CTO no longer does code review. He reviews prototypes instead. Jiaona Zhang (JZ) , CPO at Laurel (previously Dropbox, Linktree, Webflow, Airbnb), is careful about headcount, focusing on a small team where everyone ships. The friction has moved from execution to coordination. The harder problem now is how humans coordinate with their agents, how pods coordinate with each other, and how to productize what these small teams can suddenly create in weeks instead of months. Where do you sit, and what are you optimizing for? And: what's your secret talent and passion project?

I turned 30+ transcripts of the Andreessen Horowitz podcast into an RPG game. You explore the world and battle the podcast guests, where they quiz you about the takeaways from their podcast episodes. Test your knowledge of VC, AI, entrepreneurship, and tech through the battles. Win 3 of 5 questions to capture the guest and add them to your Pokédex. It's a criminally underrated podcast, and I think gaming is one of the best ways to engage with longform content. Guests you can battle include Fei-Fei Li Nicole Brichtova Justine Moore Olivia Moore Anish Acharya Mati Staniszewski Andrew Chen and more! Play it here: https://lnkd.in/ggSziDWk Inspired by the game Ben Shih built; learn how he built it here: https://lnkd.in/gAjM5xSp You can just build things!! 🔨 PS I built this with openclaw + claude API (~1.5M tokens out) + gemini + nano banana + gpt API + claude dispatch + suno

Sonder is my favorite word. It's this realization that every person around you is living a life as rich and complex as your own. I've been thinking about this for a while: I haven’t found a system that actually knows who I am. I use a dozen apps that each get a sliver of me. What I buy, what I listen to, where I swipe, but nothing connects the dots and knows who I am as a whole person. So I built Sondar. You talk to it. It picks up on who you are from your own words. And it finds you products, people, and experiences, all from one place that you own and control. The name is a play on sonder and sonar: deeply seeing people and picking up on subtle signals. It's very early. The intelligence is v1 and will get sharper. But the platform is live, letting people off the waitlist as they come. Check it out and tell me what hits and what doesn't. Feedback directly shapes where it's going next, and DMs are open. sondar.me
